subject: Assessing invariance and factor means across continuous groups

messages.author: 958db91595844d16
messages.subject: Assessing invariance and factor means across continuous groups
parts:
I want to investigate how factor means change from age 11-18. For some factors, I expect a non-linear change in factor means, so I don't want to just create two groups (e.g., 11-14 and 15-18). I expect ages 11-12 to be similar to ages 16-18, with a slight depression in factor means ages 13-14. 

I have found some information on comparing multiple groups, but I am wondering if anyone is familiar with how I could analyse change in factor means in a continuous way. I guess I could test for invariance between these groups and then plot the factor means for each individual age. Wondering if there is a better way.

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Assessing invariance and factor means across continuous groups
parts:
What you are looking for is longitudinal measurement invariance. You do the configural, weak, and strong invariance tests across time instead of groups. Once strong invariance has been established you can test mean chnage over time by either comparing means or doing a growth curve model of the factor means

You can check the following books, I believe Little has lavaan code examples, while Grimm and McArdle have OpenMx code examples fro R

Grimm, K. J., Ram, N., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Growth Modeling: Structural Equation and Multilevel Modeling Approaches. New York, NY, US.
Little, T. D. (2013). Longitudinal Structural Equation Modeling. New York, NY, US: The Guilford Press.
McArdle, J. J., & Nesselroade, J. R. (2014). Longitudinal data analysis using structural equation models. https://doi.org/10.1037/14440-000

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: Assessing invariance and factor means across continuous groups
parts:
Further to Mauricio's answer
McCardle argues in repeated measures data it is sufficient to have configural and metric invariance between times. His view is that as events change things over time it is likely that the item intercepts should change as a consequence of those events. Hence, requiring strong invariance might not be necessary. see
McArdle, J. J. (2007). Five steps in the structural factor analysis of longitudinal data. In R. Cudeck & R. C. MacCallum (Eds.), Factor analysis at 100: Historical developments and future directions (pp. 99-130). Mahwah, NJ: LEA.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Assessing invariance and factor means across continuous groups
parts: Why would strong invariance not be required? I could not follow McCardle's point in that chapter.

I don't think that chapter makes such a suggestion.  I searched for "intercept" and the only times that word appears in the chapter are in the context of change-score factor models, not the longitudinal factor model under discussion here.  If Gavin provides a quote with page number, I'd be happy to reconsider the point, but I expect it was taken out of context.  McArdle mentions (p. 120) comparing the loading matrix for latent intercepts and latent slopes in a factor-of-curves model, and how that could possibly be generalized to testing invariance in the common-factor model; perhaps that is what Gavin was referring to?
